front: Is OAuth2 an authentication protocol or an authorization protocol?
back: Authorization: it lets a client obtain limited access to a resource on a user's behalf, without necessarily proving who the user is.
accepted_answers: Authorization: it lets a client obtain limited access to a resource on a user's behalf, without necessarily proving who the user is.
hint: It answers "what can this client do," not "who is this person."

front: What are the four core roles defined in OAuth2?
back: Resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server.
accepted_answers: ["Resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server","resource owner client authorization server resource server"]
hint: One owns data, one wants access, one issues tokens, one hosts the protected data.

front: Why does OAuth2 alone not prove a user's identity to the client application?
back: OAuth2 only issues an access token scoped to some permissions; it does not define a standard way for the client to learn who the resource owner actually is, which is why OpenID Connect was built on top of it.
accepted_answers: OAuth2 only issues an access token scoped to some permissions; it does not define a standard way for the client to learn who the resource owner actually is, which is why OpenID Connect was built on top of it.
hint: Getting access to data is not the same as being told whose data it is.

front: What does OpenID Connect (OIDC) add on top of OAuth2?
back: An ID token (a signed JWT with claims about the authenticated user, such as subject and issuer) and a standardized way for the client to verify the user's identity, layered on OAuth2's authorization flows.
accepted_answers: An ID token (a signed JWT with claims about the authenticated user, such as subject and issuer) and a standardized way for the client to verify the user's identity, layered on OAuth2's authorization flows.
hint: OIDC is the identity layer OAuth2 was missing.

front: Which OAuth2 grant type is recommended for a server-side web application that can securely store a client secret?
back: Authorization code grant.
accepted_answers: ["Authorization code grant","authorization code"]
hint: It's the classic redirect-and-exchange-a-code flow.

front: Why do public clients (mobile apps, single-page apps) use the authorization code flow with PKCE instead of the plain authorization code flow?
back: Public clients cannot safely store a client secret, so PKCE adds a per-request code verifier/challenge pair that proves the app exchanging the code is the same one that started the flow, protecting against interception of the authorization code.
accepted_answers: Public clients cannot safely store a client secret, so PKCE adds a per-request code verifier/challenge pair that proves the app exchanging the code is the same one that started the flow, protecting against interception of the authorization code.
hint: No secret to prove identity, so prove it with a one-time verifier instead.

front: In the OAuth2 authorization code flow, what threat does the "state" parameter defend against?
back: Cross-site request forgery on the redirect callback: the client generates a random state value, and after redirect verifies the returned state matches, ensuring the authorization response corresponds to a request it actually initiated.
accepted_answers: Cross-site request forgery on the redirect callback: the client generates a random state value, and after redirect verifies the returned state matches, ensuring the authorization response corresponds to a request it actually initiated.
hint: It ties the callback back to a request the client itself started.

front: Why must an authorization server strictly validate the redirect_uri against a pre-registered allowlist rather than accepting any value the client sends?
back: An attacker who can redirect the authorization code (or token) to an arbitrary URI could steal it and impersonate the legitimate user's session at the client application.
accepted_answers: An attacker who can redirect the authorization code (or token) to an arbitrary URI could steal it and impersonate the legitimate user's session at the client application.
hint: A loose redirect_uri check turns the flow into an open redirect vulnerability.

front: Which OAuth2 grant type is appropriate for service-to-service authentication with no end user involved at all?
back: Client credentials grant.
accepted_answers: ["Client credentials grant","client credentials"]
hint: There is no resource owner to redirect; the service itself is the client.

front: What does an OAuth2 refresh token let a client do that an access token alone cannot?
back: Obtain a new access token after the current one expires, without requiring the resource owner to re-authenticate and re-authorize the client from scratch.
accepted_answers: Obtain a new access token after the current one expires, without requiring the resource owner to re-authenticate and re-authorize the client from scratch.
hint: It renews access without repeating the user's login.

front: Why do production systems typically use short-lived access tokens paired with longer-lived refresh tokens, instead of one long-lived access token?
back: A short expiry limits the damage window if an access token leaks, since it becomes useless soon after, while the refresh token (used less often and more tightly protected) lets the client keep getting fresh access tokens without repeated user logins.
accepted_answers: A short expiry limits the damage window if an access token leaks, since it becomes useless soon after, while the refresh token (used less often and more tightly protected) lets the client keep getting fresh access tokens without repeated user logins.
hint: Short-lived tokens shrink the blast radius of a leaked token.

front: What is refresh token rotation, and what security property does it add?
back: Each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a brand-new refresh token and invalidates the old one; if an old, already-rotated refresh token is ever presented again, that signals theft/replay and the server can revoke the whole token family.
accepted_answers: Each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a brand-new refresh token and invalidates the old one; if an old, already-rotated refresh token is ever presented again, that signals theft/replay and the server can revoke the whole token family.
hint: A reused "old" refresh token is a red flag that someone else has a copy.

front: What are the three dot-separated parts of a JWT?
back: Header, payload (claims), and signature.
accepted_answers: ["Header, payload, signature","header payload signature"]
hint: Each part is base64url-encoded and separated by a period.

front: Why is it insecure for a resource server to trust a JWT's claims without verifying its signature?
back: Anyone can construct a JWT with arbitrary claims (including base64-decoding and editing an existing one), so without signature verification against the issuer's known public key, a forged token with fabricated permissions would be accepted as genuine.
accepted_answers: Anyone can construct a JWT with arbitrary claims (including base64-decoding and editing an existing one), so without signature verification against the issuer's known public key, a forged token with fabricated permissions would be accepted as genuine.
hint: Readable is not the same as trustworthy; only the signature proves authenticity.

front: What does the "aud" (audience) claim in a JWT protect against if properly validated?
back: Token replay across services: a token issued for one specific resource server should be rejected by a different resource server, even though the signature itself is valid, if that server is not in the token's intended audience.
accepted_answers: Token replay across services: a token issued for one specific resource server should be rejected by a different resource server, even though the signature itself is valid, if that server is not in the token's intended audience.
hint: A valid signature only proves who issued it, not who it was meant for.

front: What is a JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) endpoint used for?
back: It publishes the authorization server's current public signing keys (with key IDs) so resource servers can fetch them and verify JWT signatures without a shared secret, and can pick up rotated keys automatically.
accepted_answers: It publishes the authorization server's current public signing keys (with key IDs) so resource servers can fetch them and verify JWT signatures without a shared secret, and can pick up rotated keys automatically.
hint: It lets verifiers fetch the current public keys instead of hardcoding one.

front: Why is revoking a single, already-issued, self-contained JWT before its expiration difficult compared to a server-side session?
back: The JWT's claims are self-contained and independently verifiable by any resource server via signature alone, so unless every verifier also checks a revocation/deny list on every request, an "invalidated" token remains valid until it naturally expires.
accepted_answers: The JWT's claims are self-contained and independently verifiable by any resource server via signature alone, so unless every verifier also checks a revocation/deny list on every request, an "invalidated" token remains valid until it naturally expires.
hint: Statelessness that helps performance also makes early revocation harder.

front: A resource server rejects otherwise-valid JWTs from a different but legitimate server because their clocks differ by a few seconds around the token's "exp" or "nbf" time. What is the usual fix?
back: Allow a small clock-skew tolerance (a leeway of a few seconds to a couple of minutes) when validating time-based claims, since perfectly synchronized clocks across independent systems cannot be assumed.
accepted_answers: Allow a small clock-skew tolerance (a leeway of a few seconds to a couple of minutes) when validating time-based claims, since perfectly synchronized clocks across independent systems cannot be assumed.
hint: Real clocks drift; time-based validation needs some tolerance.

front: What is an OAuth2 "scope"?
back: A string representing a specific permission or capability being requested/granted (for example, "read:orders"), which the resource server can check against before allowing an action, distinct from the user's overall identity or role.
accepted_answers: A string representing a specific permission or capability being requested/granted (for example, "read:orders"), which the resource server can check against before allowing an action, distinct from the user's overall identity or role.
hint: Scopes describe "what this token can do," narrower than the user's full identity.

front: What is token introspection used for, and when is it especially necessary compared to just decoding a JWT?
back: An endpoint on the authorization server that a resource server calls to check whether a token is currently valid and get its metadata; it is necessary for opaque (non-self-contained) tokens that cannot simply be decoded and locally verified.
accepted_answers: An endpoint on the authorization server that a resource server calls to check whether a token is currently valid and get its metadata; it is necessary for opaque (non-self-contained) tokens that cannot simply be decoded and locally verified.
hint: Opaque tokens need to ask the issuer directly; JWTs can often be checked locally.

front: What is the key trade-off between opaque access tokens and self-contained JWT access tokens?
back: Opaque tokens require a network call (introspection) to the authorization server on every validation but can be revoked immediately; JWTs can be verified locally without a network call for speed, but are harder to revoke before they expire.
accepted_answers: Opaque tokens require a network call (introspection) to the authorization server on every validation but can be revoked immediately; JWTs can be verified locally without a network call for speed, but are harder to revoke before they expire.
hint: Fast-but-hard-to-revoke versus slower-but-instantly-revocable.

front: What is mutual TLS (mTLS) used for in service-to-service authentication?
back: Both the client service and the server service present and verify each other's TLS certificates, so each side cryptographically proves its identity to the other, not just the server proving its identity to the client as in normal TLS.
accepted_answers: Both the client service and the server service present and verify each other's TLS certificates, so each side cryptographically proves its identity to the other, not just the server proving its identity to the client as in normal TLS.
hint: Normal TLS proves the server's identity; mTLS makes the client prove its identity too.

front: In a service mesh (such as Istio or Linkerd), why is mTLS between services often handled by sidecar proxies instead of application code?
back: The sidecar intercepts and encrypts traffic transparently, issuing and rotating short-lived certificates automatically, so individual services don't each need to implement certificate management and mutual authentication themselves.
accepted_answers: The sidecar intercepts and encrypts traffic transparently, issuing and rotating short-lived certificates automatically, so individual services don't each need to implement certificate management and mutual authentication themselves.
hint: Push a cross-cutting concern into shared infrastructure instead of every service reimplementing it.

front: What is the key difference between a static API key and an OAuth2 access token for authenticating a service call?
back: An API key is typically a long-lived, coarse-grained shared secret with no built-in expiry or standardized scoping, while an OAuth2 access token is normally short-lived, scoped to specific permissions, and issued through a standardized flow that supports rotation and auditing.
accepted_answers: An API key is typically a long-lived, coarse-grained shared secret with no built-in expiry or standardized scoping, while an OAuth2 access token is normally short-lived, scoped to specific permissions, and issued through a standardized flow that supports rotation and auditing.
hint: API keys are usually "forever and everything"; OAuth2 tokens are usually "briefly and specifically."

front: What is the difference between an OAuth2 confidential client and a public client?
back: A confidential client can securely store a secret (for example, a backend server), while a public client cannot reliably keep a secret confidential (for example, a mobile app or single-page app running on a user's device), which changes which grant types and protections it should use.
accepted_answers: A confidential client can securely store a secret (for example, a backend server), while a public client cannot reliably keep a secret confidential (for example, a mobile app or single-page app running on a user's device), which changes which grant types and protections it should use.
hint: Can it keep a secret? That answers what flow it should use.

front: Why are the OAuth2 implicit grant and resource owner password credentials grant now discouraged in favor of authorization code with PKCE?
back: The implicit grant exposes access tokens directly in the browser URL fragment with no client authentication, and the password grant requires the client to directly handle the user's raw credentials; both have weaker security properties than a code-exchange flow with PKCE.
accepted_answers: The implicit grant exposes access tokens directly in the browser URL fragment with no client authentication, and the password grant requires the client to directly handle the user's raw credentials; both have weaker security properties than a code-exchange flow with PKCE.
hint: Both older grants expose more sensitive material to more parties than necessary.

front: An internal microservice calls another internal microservice on behalf of an authenticated end user, and the downstream service needs to know which user's request this is. What is a common way to carry that context forward safely?
back: Propagate the user's original access token (or a derived, appropriately scoped token) along the call chain, so downstream services can validate it and see the same subject/claims rather than the caller asserting the user's identity unverified.
accepted_answers: Propagate the user's original access token (or a derived, appropriately scoped token) along the call chain, so downstream services can validate it and see the same subject/claims rather than the caller asserting the user's identity unverified.
hint: Forward a verifiable token, not just a trusted claim from the calling service.
